summary: An island nation in the western Pacific made up of more than three hundred islands, known for the Rock Islands and as a diving destination; it became independent in 1994, concluded a Compact of Free Association with the United States, and is a diplomatic ally of the Republic of China (Taiwan).

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was introduced in 1891 by Spanish Capuchin missionaries, when Palau belonged to the Spanish Caroline Islands. After Germany purchased Palau in 1899, German Capuchins took over, and during the Japanese rule after World War I Spanish Jesuits continued the mission. Because Catholicism has the longest missionary history in Palau and established schools in places such as Koror, it became the largest religion in Palau.

ranking.name: Evangelical Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism first entered during the German period, when the German Liebenzell Mission arrived around 1929; missionary work was restricted during the Japanese period. After the US military occupation in 1944 and American trusteeship, American evangelical churches expanded their influence, with the Palau Evangelical Church the main one, and today it is the second largest religious group.

ranking.name: Seventh-day Adventist Church
ranking.description: The Seventh-day Adventist Church arrived in the first half of the 20th century and expanded during the American trusteeship after World War II. It is known for running schools, and the Adventist school in Koror is one of Palau's important English-language educational institutions, which has also attracted some followers.

ranking.name: Modekngei
ranking.description: Modekngei is Palau's indigenous religion, founded around 1915 during the Japanese period by the prophet Temedad and others; it blends traditional ancestral spirit beliefs with elements of Christianity, and at first had a character of resistance against Japanese colonial rule, for which it was suppressed by the Japanese authorities. It is an important force in preserving traditional Palauan culture, and its followers are concentrated on the island of Babeldaob.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was brought mainly by migrant workers from Bangladesh, who came to Palau after the 1990s to work in construction and services. There are almost no Muslims among Palauan citizens, so the proportion is low, and followers are mainly concentrated in Koror.

religion.background: Palauans traditionally believed in ancestral spirits and village guardian deities. At the end of the 19th century Spanish missionaries brought Catholicism, and Germany and then Japan ruled in succession; during the Japanese period the indigenous religion Modekngei, combining tradition with Christianity, appeared. In 1944 the US military occupied Palau, and after World War II it was administered by the United States as a United Nations trust territory, and Protestantism and other denominations expanded. After independence in 1994 it concluded a Compact of Free Association with the United States, and the religion is predominantly Christian.

language.official: The official languages are Palauan and English.

ranking.name: Palauan
ranking.description: Palauan belongs to the Austronesian family and is the language of the indigenous Palauans. It had no writing before the 19th century, and missionaries recorded it in the Latin alphabet. During Japanese rule (1914–1944) Japanese-language education was promoted, but Palauan continued in the home; after independence in 1994 Palauan and English became co-official languages, and Palauan is mainly used in homes and communities. Palauan retains many Japanese and English loanwords.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English became the language of schools, government and commerce during the American trusteeship of 1947–1994. After independence in 1994 the Compact of Free Association with the United States allowed Palauans to travel freely to the US to work and study, so English is very widespread in Palau, and government documents, law and higher education are mainly in English.

ranking.name: Filipino
ranking.description: Filipino is mainly used by the Filipino migrant workers who came to Palau in large numbers after the 1980s, working in construction, tourism, domestic service and healthcare. Because Palau's population is only about twenty thousand, the proportion of foreign workers is very high, and Filipinos are the largest foreign group.

ranking.name: Chinese
ranking.description: Chinese is mainly used by foreign workers and businesspeople from mainland China and Taiwan. Since Palau established diplomatic relations with Taiwan in 1999, the two countries have had close exchanges, and there are quite a few Chinese speakers in tourism, fishing and the restaurant industry.

language.history: Palauan belongs to the Austronesian family and was originally an oral language. From 1885 Spain claimed rule, in 1899 it was sold to Germany, and in 1914 Japan occupied it and promoted Japanese-language education, and Palauan absorbed a large number of Japanese words. From 1947 it was under American trusteeship, and English became the language of education and administration. After independence in 1994, Palauan and English were made co-official languages, and Angaur State has also designated Japanese as one of its official state languages.

ranking.name: Taro
ranking.description: Whole taro is boiled or steamed and peeled, then cut into pieces or mashed, sometimes with coconut milk added, giving a creamy texture; it is often eaten with fish or meat.
ranking.history: Taro is Palau's most important traditional staple, grown in wetland taro patches and brought thousands of years ago by Austronesian navigators. In Palau's matrilineal society, taro patches are managed and cultivated by women, and growing good taro is a symbol of a woman's status. At traditional ceremonies such as weddings, funerals and childbirth celebrations, women exchange large quantities of taro as gifts, symbolizing the wealth and relationships between families.

ranking.name: Coconut crab
ranking.description: The large land-dwelling coconut crab is steamed or stewed in coconut milk, and the crab meat and roe have a sweet coconut flavor; it is regarded as a precious delicacy for entertaining guests.
ranking.history: The coconut crab is a large land-dwelling crustacean of the Pacific islands that can crack open coconuts with its powerful large claws, hence its name. In Palau it is a treasured dish served to honored guests at traditional feasts. Because of overharvesting, the Palauan government has legislated size limits for catching and prohibited the taking of egg-bearing females, and some restaurants also restrict its sale, in order to protect this slow-growing species.

ranking.name: Sashimi
ranking.description: Fresh raw fish such as tuna is cut into thin slices and eaten raw dipped in soy sauce and wasabi; it is a common dish in Palauan restaurants, homes and feasts.
ranking.history: During Japanese rule of Palau from 1914 to 1944, large numbers of Japanese settlers came to Palau, and Koror was then the administrative center of the Japanese South Seas Government, so Palauans adopted many Japanese eating habits. These habits were retained after the war, and sashimi, miso soup and rice balls are still quite common in Palau today, reflecting the profound influence of Japanese rule on Palauan culture.

ranking.name: Tapioca (cassava)
ranking.description: Cassava is boiled and eaten, or ground into flour and mixed with coconut milk and sugar to make a dessert, with a soft, chewy texture and a coconut aroma; it is a common home-style snack.
ranking.history: Cassava originated in South America and was introduced to the Pacific islands after the 19th century by Europeans and through development during the Japanese period. Because it is drought-tolerant and easy to grow, it gradually became an important source of starch in Palau besides taro. Desserts made from cassava and coconut milk often appear at family gatherings, church events and traditional celebrations, and are an everyday snack for Palauans.

ranking.name: Breadfruit
ranking.description: Whole breadfruit is roasted in a fire or cut into pieces and boiled, with a texture similar to potato or bread; it can be eaten with fish and coconut milk, and can also be made into chips.
ranking.history: Breadfruit is a traditional staple of the Pacific islands, spread among the islands thousands of years ago by Austronesian navigators. It bears abundant fruit, with a single tree producing hundreds of fruits a year, making it an important source of food. In Palau, the breadfruit season is a time when families share food; in recent years the Westernization of diets has led to increases in obesity and diabetes, and the government and communities encourage a return to eating traditional crops.
